newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel resumes construction despite warnings.
newsitem.headline: Israel resumes construction despite warnings.

text.p: Israeli bulldozers ripped into an Arab East Jerusalem hillside on Wednesday for the second day to build a new Jewish settlement despite international criticism.

Israeli forces remained on high alert for Palestinian violence in response to the project they say violates peace accords with the Jewish state. A brief confrontation near the site on Tuesday ended without casualties.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected criticism of Israel's plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews on land between Jerusalem and Bethlehem it captured in the 1967 Middle East war, saying it was part of the Israeli capital.
"I can't imagine any peace process under which we can't build in our capital," he told Israel Radio on Wednesday. "I don't agree to any peace that prevents us from building in Jerusalem."
Netanyahu's cabinet approved the project despite warnings from Palestinians, who see the east of Jerusalem as their future capital, and Israeli security officials of widespread unrest.
The United States, Israel's closest ally, said on Tuesday peace efforts could be crushed by the Israeli project. Officials in Washington urged Israel and the Palestinians to resume talks.
The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) called for an immediate meeting of the United Nations Security Council to demand a halt to the settlement.

Netanyahu rejected a U.S. denial of his charge that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had given Islamic militants the green light to resume bombings such as suicide attacks that killed scores of Israelis a year ago.

U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said: "We have not seen any evidence that Chairman Arafat has given the green light to anybody to incite violence in Jerusalem or the West Bank or the Gaza Strip. On the contrary, we have recent assurances from Chairman Arafat that he stands against violence."
But Netanyahu said on Wednesday: "We have solid information from the Israeli intelligence. We see contacts of the PLO with Hamas and other organisations," he told Israel Radio.
"I want to say clearly. If there is terrorism we will see the Palestinian Authority as responsible."

Netanyahu dismissed as "stupid" a suggestion by the Israel Radio interviewer he wanted confrontation with the Palestinians to end the Israel-PLO 1993 Oslo peace accords, which Netanyahu had opposed until shortly before his election in 1996.
Arafat aide Yasser Abed Rabbo said after a consultation of the Palestinian leadership late on Tuesday the settlement could be "a fatal strike to the peace process."

"The Israeli government wants to impose facts on the ground through settlement in Jabel Abu Ghneim and around Jerusalem in order to cut and divide the West Bank to two parts so that it cannot have any opportunity to negotiate about the final status," Abed Rabbo told reporters.
Jabel Abu Ghneim is the Arabic name for the settlement site Israel calls Har Homa.
The PLO's U.N. observer, Nasser al-Kidwa, said the Security Council had a duty to act.

"We call upon the Security Council to convene an immediate, official meeting to consider this serious situation, and to adopt a resolution in this regard, clearly demanding the immediate and full cessation of all settlement activities in Jabal Abu Ghneim, East Jerusalem and throughout the occupied Palestinian territory," he said.

The request is likely to be considered on Wednesday. The 185-member U.N. General Assembly adopted a resolution-- opposed by only Israel and the United States -- last Thursday calling on Israel to stop settlement activities. That followed a U.S. veto on March 7 of a similar resolution in the Security Council.
